model_classification.evidence_quote: Physiologically-based pharmacokinetic (PBPK) models were developed for PFOA & PFOS for the gestation and lactation life stages in humans

model_context.stated_purpose: to understand how the physiological changes associated with development affect pharmacokinetics of these compounds in the mother, fetus, and infant
model_context.dose_metric: total plasma AUC in the mother and fetus (at embryonic week 39) for the gestation models or the total maternal plasma AUC and infant body AUC (at 6 months postpartum) for the lactation models
model_context.current_application: estimating maternal exposure and internal dose in fetus and infant
model_context.source_quote: These models were derived from PBPK models for PFOA/PFOS that were previously developed for adult humans and rats during gestation and lactation and from existing human pregnancy and lactation models developed for other chemicals.

adme_determinant_evidence.description: Renal resorption is responsible for long half-lives of PFAAs in humans
adme_determinant_evidence.evidence_quote: Renal reabsorption is thought to be responsible for the long half-lives observed in humans and other species

adme_determinant_evidence.description: Free fraction of chemical in plasma controls tissue uptake and filtration
adme_determinant_evidence.evidence_quote: the free fraction of chemical controls how much chemical will be available for tissue uptake or filtration

adme_determinant_evidence.description: Flow to filtrate compartment (QFil; analogous to GFR) affects elimination rate
adme_determinant_evidence.evidence_quote: the flow to the filtrate compartment will affect how quickly the chemical is eliminated

adme_phase_evidence.biological_mechanism: Amniotic fluid compartment included based on rat data showing PFAAs present in amniotic fluid
adme_phase_evidence.mathematical_implementation: Simple diffusion described by ktrans3C and ktrans4C
adme_phase_evidence.evidence_quote: Data in rats showed that PFAAs are present in amniotic fluid ; thus, an amniotic fluid compartment was included in the rat models and also in the human models presented here. Transfer rates between the amniotic fluid compartment and the fetal body are described as simple diffusion (ktrans3C and ktrans4C; Table 3 ).

adme_phase_evidence.biological_mechanism: Renal resorption via saturable transport (Tm, Kt)
adme_phase_evidence.mathematical_implementation: Michaelis-Menten kinetics with Tm and Kt parameters
adme_phase_evidence.evidence_quote: The fetal plasma AUC is also affected by the maternal renal resorption parameters (Tm and Kt) as these will determine how much chemical is eliminated from the maternal system rather than being available for transfer to the fetus.
the bidirectional placental transfer rate constants (ktrans1c and ktrans2c)

adme_phase_evidence.biological_mechanism: Transfer from breast milk to nursing infant
adme_phase_evidence.evidence_quote: KmilkC will determine how quickly the chemical is then transferred from breast milk to the nursing infant

stated_assumptions.description: Volumes of liver, kidney, filtrate, and gut remain constant fractions of prepregnancy maternal body weight
stated_assumptions.evidence_quote: Volumes of liver, kidney, filtrate, and gut remained constant fractions of the prepregnancy (non-pregnant) maternal body weight (BWinit)

stated_assumptions.description: Filtrate compartment set at 10% of kidney volume
stated_assumptions.evidence_quote: The filtrate compartment, as in the adult human model, was set at 10% of the kidney volume (the model is not sensitive to this value).

stated_assumptions.description: Mammary tissue volume changes during lactation are lumped with remaining maternal tissue volume
stated_assumptions.evidence_quote: Because the volume of mammary tissue changes during lactation, these volume changes were accounted for by lumping this change in volume in with the remaining maternal tissue volume.

stated_assumptions.description: Renal plasma flow assumed to be approximately 5 times GFR during lactation
stated_assumptions.evidence_quote: Since there were no available data on renal plasma flow changes during lactation, renal plasma flow was assumed to be approximately 5 times that of the GFR (GFR is normally approximately 20% of renal plasma flow).

stated_assumptions.description: Maternal PFOA and PFOS exposure modeled as generic input to plasma compartment (IV)
stated_assumptions.evidence_quote: maternal PFOA and PFOS exposure was modeled as a generic input to the plasma compartment (designated as “IV” in Figures 1 and 2 ) as contributions of PFAA exposure from different exposure routes are not well understood
stated_assumptions.source_location: Exposure estimation and predictions of internal dose for general population

stated_assumptions.description: Constant exposure assumed over 24 hour time period for lactation exposure estimates
stated_assumptions.evidence_quote: assuming constant exposure over a 24 hour time period

assumption_evidence.stated_assumption: Mammary tissue volume changes during lactation lumped with remaining maternal tissue volume

assumption_evidence.structural_impact: Reduces number of explicitly tracked compartments; mammary volume change absorbed into general maternal tissue
assumption_evidence.evidence_quote: Because the volume of mammary tissue changes during lactation, these volume changes were accounted for by lumping this change in volume in with the remaining maternal tissue volume.
